topic: Neural Networks: The Blueprint of Artificial Intelligence

sections.title: The Biological Inspiration: The Puppy Analogy
sections.content: Introduction to the concept of a neural network as a system that learns from experience. We compare the artificial network to a puppy learning to distinguish between a 'ball' and a 'lemon' based on sensory inputs.
sections.example: A digital puppy character named 'Pixel' receives inputs like color (yellow vs. red) and shape (round vs. oval) to decide if an object is a toy or a snack.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Linear Equation as a Slider
sections.content: Before diving into neurons, we revisit the basic linear formula y = wx + b. We visualize 'w' (weight) as the strength of a signal and 'b' (bias) as the threshold for a decision.
sections.example: A visual slider where increasing 'w' makes the line steeper (more sensitive to input) and shifting 'b' moves the line up or down (changing the baseline tendency).

sections.title: The Artificial Neuron: The Mathematical Heart
sections.content: Anatomy of a single neuron. It performs a weighted sum of inputs followed by an activation function. We visually represent the summation as a funnel and the activation as a gatekeeper.
sections.example: Graphical representation of the Sigmoid or ReLU function: A 'S-curve' graph that shows how the neuron 'fires' (output near 1) only when the input math exceeds a certain pressure.

sections.title: Layered Architecture: The Assembly Line
sections.content: Explaining how neurons organize into Input, Hidden, and Output layers. Data flows from left to right, becoming more abstract at each stage.
sections.example: An image of a '7' is broken into raw pixels (Input), identifies edges and corners (Hidden), and finally outputs the probability of the digit being '7' (Output).

sections.title: The Math of Connectivity: Matrix Multiplication
sections.content: How layers communicate. Instead of calculating one-by-one, we use matrices to calculate all neurons in a layer simultaneously. Visualizing the 'dot product' as a grid of connections.
sections.example: An animated grid (Matrix W) multiplying by a vector (Input X) where the intersections glow brighter based on the strength of the connection (weight).

sections.title: Learning via Feedback: The Error Correction
sections.content: Briefly introducing Loss Functions and Backpropagation. The network compares its guess to the truth and 'wiggles' the weights to reduce error. This is the 'learning' phase.
sections.example: Pixel the Puppy guesses 'Lemon' for a 'Ball.' A 'Heatmap' appears on the network, showing which weights caused the mistake, and they physically shrink or grow to fix it for next time.
